fetched_contents.text: Varying rotational speeds and their effect on the mechanical properties of friction stir welded 6082-T651 aluminium alloy plates 1. Introduction In recent years,friction stir welding has been widely utilized since it has proven to be a solid-state joining process that is environmentally friendly and cost effective [1]. The welding process involves no metal melting or crystallization which avoids welding defects such as blowholes and burning through from the source and the welding remains intact [2], [3], [4]. The current study puts the focus on the effect of changing rotational speeds on the resulting mechanical properties of 6082-T651 aluminium alloy plates. The tool rotational speeds are responsible for the heating and mixing of the alloy plates getting welded. The change in rotational speed influences the resulting mechanical properties of the weld area, and this study investigates how much this influences the resulting mechanical properties. Rotation speed is the rate at which the tool rotates around its axis and is one important parameter in FSW. It is directly related to the increase of the processing temperature and can be manipulated to increase welding travel speeds. The increase of the rotation speed results in a higher processing speed and consequently higher cooling rates [5]. For this study the welding speed, tool tilt angle and plunge depth were kept constant to properly assess the influence a change in rotational speed has on the resulting mechanical properties. The welding or traverse speed is also crucial in Friction Stir Welding as it influences the resulting underlying physical properties of the material. One important condition linked to welding speed is the peak process temperature. That peak process temperature increases with decreasing weld travel speed as well as increasing rotation speed of the tool. Heat input can be assumed to be inversely proportional to welding speed, so if we want to increase the welding speed, its needed to increase rotation speed to keep the temperature needed for the operation. High welding speed has been proved to increase stresses and wear on the tool. These can lead to an increased incidence of defects and require repairs or deliver scrapped components. Meaning that the optimum welding speed is therefore not normally the fastest possible speed. Another issue as the welding speed increases is the requirement for tighter process tolerances, this results in more investment in joint preparation and fit up [5]. The axial force (sometimes known as downward force or tools plunge force) is directly related to the plunge depth, the deeper the heel plunge depth, the higher the axial force [5]. The tilt angle is the angle between the centerline of the tool and the line perpendicular to the surface of the workpiece, opposite to the direction of welding [6]. A featureless shoulder employs a tilt angle leaning backwards in respect of the welding path, which means there is more open room in front of the tool, and the back of the tool does the forging of material behind the pin [7]. The tool tilt angle was kept constant for all the welds undertaken in this study. The rotational speed was varied but the welding speed kept constant to track changes in the mechanical properties of friction stir welded 6082-T6 aluminium alloy plates. The tool shoulder was kept constant as one welding tool was used for the duration of this study. 1.1. Material characteristics The accompanying tables show the chemical composition, the physical and mechanical properties of 6082-T651 aluminium alloy plates. These assist in comparing the effect of the welding process on the underlying physical and mechanical properties. The material used in this study was 6082-T651 aluminium alloy with a thickness of 6 mm and belongs to the Al–Mg–Si (Aluminium–Manganese–Silicon) alloys. This material is heat treatable which means that mechanical properties may be improved by the solution heat-treatment process. Al–Mg–Si alloys are widely used as a medium strength structural alloy which have additional advantages of good weldability, corrosion resistance and immunity to stress corrosion cracking. The 6XXX series are used for most extrusions, the smaller quantities being available as sheet and plate. Magnesium and silicon are added either in balanced amounts to form quasi-binary Al–Mg–Si alloys or with an excess of silicon above that needed to form Mg–Si. Al–Mg–Si alloys are normally aged at approximately 170 °C. ### Which parameters are most strongly correlated with tensile strength?
The evidence suggests that rotational speed is among the most important parameters. A search result states that “as the rotational speed and pin diameter increase, the input heat increases, resulting in higher tensile strength” [N2-R3]. Another study on friction stir welding parameters explicitly notes that “tool rotational speed, welding speed, and shoulder diameter” are evaluated for their effect on ultimate tensile strength [N5-R1]. A separate study reports that “an increase in the rotational speed increased the ultimate tensile strength and microhardness of the specimens” [N6-R3]. These together indicate that rotational speed is a major driver of tensile strength, especially when paired with a controlled or moderate welding speed.

Axial force is also important. The same search result notes that “the authors observe that rotational speed and axial force are significant factors in tensile strength and microhardness” [N3-R2], and the broader FSW literature emphasizes that axial force influences tool longevity, process efficiency, and weld integrity [N1-R3]. While the evidence here does not give a direct numerical ranking of the relative importance of each parameter, it clearly supports axial force as a significant factor, especially when combined with rotational speed.

Welding speed is a secondary but still important parameter. One study notes that welding speed is “crucial in Friction Stir Welding as it influences the resulting underlying physical properties of the material” [N2-F1], and another emphasizes that “the increase of the rotation speed results in a higher processing speed and consequently higher cooling rates” [N2-F1]. In a comparison study, welding speed is explicitly listed as one of the optimized parameters affecting tensile strength, yield strength, and hardness [N5-R1]. So welding speed matters, but its effect is often indirect: it interacts with rotational speed to control heat input and cooling rate, which in turn affect microstructure and strength [N2-F1][N4-R4].

### How rotation speed, travel speed, and axial force interact
The interaction is best understood as a tradeoff between heat input, cooling rate, and mechanical load. Rotational speed dominates the heat generation and mixing behavior. The 6082-T651 aluminum study states that rotational speed is “directly related to the increase of the processing temperature” and that increasing rotational speed can increase welding travel speeds while also increasing cooling rates [N2-F1]. In other words, higher rotation speed can raise peak temperature but also accelerate cooling, potentially improving strength through finer microstructure while risking defects if the cooling is too abrupt [N2-F1].

Travel speed, or welding speed, is the counterbalance. The same source says that welding speed is crucial because it influences peak process temperature: peak temperature increases with decreasing weld travel speed and increasing rotation speed [N2-F1]. Another search result says that the ratio of tool rotation speed to travel speed is used to distinguish hot welds from cold welds [N1-R5]. This implies that for a given rotational speed, lower travel speed increases heat input, whereas higher travel speed reduces it. In the aluminum study, welding speed was kept constant while rotational speed was varied, showing that rotation speed can be isolated as a dominant variable [N2-F1].

Axial force interacts primarily through forging pressure. The evidence here does not give direct tensile-strength numbers for axial force alone, but it does say that axial force is directly related to plunge depth and that tool force influences weld integrity and tool longevity [N1-R3][N1-R5]. In the context of tensile strength, axial force is likely to affect the amount of material flow, forging pressure, and defect formation rather than directly raising strength in isolation. Friction stir welding parameters strongly influence both tensile strength and microhardness in steels, but the effects are not uniform across studies and depend on the specific parameter, the weld configuration, and the resulting microstructure. The evidence points to rotational speed as the strongest single correlate of strength and hardness, while welding speed and axial force interact to control heat input, cooling rate, forging pressure, and defect formation [N2-R3][N2-F1][N3-R2][N5-R1][N6-R3]. ## 1) Which welding parameters most strongly correlate with tensile strength?

The branch reports consistently identify **rotational speed**, **welding speed**, and **axial force** as the most important parameters.

### Rotational speed
Rotational speed is the strongest single correlate of tensile strength in the evidence. One source notes that “as the rotational speed and pin diameter increase, the input heat increases, resulting in higher tensile strength” [N2-R3]. Another study reports that “an increase in the rotational speed increased the ultimate tensile strength and microhardness of the specimens” [N6-R3]. These findings suggest that higher rotation speed generally improves strength by increasing mixing, heat input, and microstructural refinement [N2-R3][N6-R3].

### Welding speed
Welding speed is important but more indirect. The evidence says welding speed is “crucial in Friction Stir Welding as it influences the resulting underlying physical properties of the material” [N2-F1]. It also notes that peak process temperature increases with decreasing weld travel speed and increasing rotation speed [N2-F1]. This means welding speed is not simply a strength booster; it controls the balance between heat input and cooling rate, and thus indirectly affects strength through microstructure and defect formation [N2-F1][N4-R4].

### Axial force
Axial force is also significant. The evidence states that “rotational speed and axial force are significant factors in tensile strength and microhardness” [N3-R2], and that axial force is directly related to plunge depth and influences weld integrity and tool longevity [N1-R3]. While the branch reports do not give a direct numerical ranking of importance, they clearly support axial force as a secondary but still important factor, especially when combined with rotational speed [N3-R2][N1-R3].

### Overall ranking
The evidence supports a hierarchy in which **rotational speed** is the strongest factor, **welding speed** is a secondary control parameter, and **axial force** is an important secondary factor [N2-R3][N2-F1][N3-R2][N5-R1][N6-R3].

This implies that the combination of high rotation speed with low travel speed raises heat input and may increase hardness, but it also raises the risk of defects if cooling is too abrupt [N2-F1][N1-R5].

In the context of tensile strength, axial force likely affects the amount of material flow, forging pressure, and defect formation rather than directly raising strength in isolation [N1-R3][N1-R5].

The strongest tensile-strength results usually occur when rotational speed and axial force are set to balance heat input and forging pressure, while welding speed is kept within a range that avoids excessive tool wear or defects [N2-F1][N5-R2].
